english_translation: A black-handled kitchen knife with a sharp pointed blade—used for cutting meat and vegetables or opening tins—rests on a tiled floor.

dialogue.shona: Banga idema, rine kumuromo kwakatesvera. Rinoshandiswa kuita mabasa akasiyana mumba yokubikira .
dialogue.english: A dark knife with a sharp point is used for various tasks in the kitchen.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akasiyana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akasiyana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('Rinoshandiswa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Rinoshandiswa' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mumba')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mumba'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: The Kitchen Knife ('Banga') & Culinary Preparation ('Mumba Yokubikira')
cultural_notes.content: In a Shona kitchen ('mumba yokubikira'), a sharp pointed utility knife ('banga rine kumuromo kwakatesvera') is indispensable for slicing beef ('nyama') and finely shredding leafy greens ('muriwo') into thin ribbons.

active_exercises.prompt: If someone says 'Ndinonzwa nyota, ndinoda kunwa mukaka kana mvura', what are they asking for?
options: Bread and sugar because it is morning
Maize meal and cooking oil from the market
Salt and vegetables for the evening meal
Milk or water because they feel thirsty
active_exercises.correct_answer: Milk or water because they feel thirsty

active_exercises.prompt: Choose the natural English meaning of this new sentence: 'Vana vanoda kudya chingwa nemukaka mangwanani.'
options: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
We bought sugar, salt, and vegetables yesterday.
Father is cooking meat and sadza for dinner tonight.
The bread has run out so I am going to the shop.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vana' = 'The children', 'vanoda kudya' = 'want to eat', 'chingwa nemukaka' = 'bread and milk', 'mangwanani' = 'in the morning'.
